items.explanation: Taylor's 'scientific management' broke jobs into timed motions to squeeze maximum output from workers — the intellectual seed of the assembly line.
options: A. Helped immigrant workers assimilate
B. Guaranteed higher wages and better conditions
C. Sought maximum efficiency in factory operations
D. Required extensive worker training
items.stem: Frederick W. Taylor's methods, embraced by many factory owners,

option_explanations.A: Taylor's system was about squeezing output from workers, not about helping immigrants assimilate. 'Scientific management' treated workers as machines to be timed and optimized, not as newcomers to be welcomed.
option_explanations.B: The opposite of how Taylorism worked in practice. Taylor's methods were meant to raise output — often by cutting wages per unit and speeding up work — not to guarantee workers higher pay or better conditions.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Frederick W. Taylor's 'scientific management' broke factory jobs into timed, standardized motions to wring maximum efficiency and output from every worker — the intellectual seed of the assembly line.
option_explanations.D: Taylor's system deskilled work on purpose: by breaking jobs into tiny, timed motions, it required less skill and less training from workers, not more.

items.explanation: Gilded Age presidential candidates were famously colorless — which is why parades, rallies, and torchlight spectacles, not personalities, drew voters into politics.
options: A. Campaign parades and rallies excited the public
B. The evenly matched parties produced close races
C. Spreading newspapers informed more voters
D. The era's presidential candidates were dynamic figures
items.stem: Americans joined the political process in this era for all of the following reasons EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Gilded Age campaigns really did excite the public — torchlight parades, rallies, and marching clubs drew huge crowds. This was a real reason Americans joined the political process, so it is not the exception.
option_explanations.B: The two parties really were evenly matched in this era, producing razor-thin elections (several presidencies were decided by a few thousand votes). Close races did drive participation, so this is not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Newspapers really did spread rapidly and inform more voters in the Gilded Age. This was a genuine cause of participation, not the exception the question asks for.
option_explanations.D: Correct — this is the exception. Gilded Age presidential candidates were famously colorless — party stalwarts like Hayes, Garfield, Arthur, and Benjamin Harrison, none of them dynamic figures. It was parades, rallies, and close races, not personalities, that drew voters in.

items.explanation: Coxey's march changed no federal policy; the reigning view that fighting depressions was not the federal government's job resembled Herbert Hoover's stance in the first years of the Great Depression.
options: A. The unemployed were becoming politically active
B. The 1890s depression hit every social class
C. The government's hands-off depression policy resembled Hoover's 1929-1932 approach
D. The march won wide press coverage
items.stem: Coxey's Army's 1894 march on Washington demonstrates that

option_explanations.A: The unemployed were politically active in many ways, but the question asks what the march demonstrates — and Coxey's Army changed no federal policy. Activity alone is not the point; the government's non-response is.
option_explanations.B: The 1890s depression hit working people hardest — unemployment soared while many elites weathered it. It did not hit every social class equally, and the march demonstrates the government's hands-off stance, not the depression's breadth.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Coxey's 1894 march of the unemployed on Washington won attention but changed no federal policy — the reigning view was that fighting depressions was not the federal government's job, a stance closely resembling Herbert Hoover's hands-off approach in the first years of the Great Depression (1929–1932).
option_explanations.D: The march did get press coverage, but coverage alone is not what it demonstrates historically. What matters is that a national protest of the unemployed produced no federal action — the government's inaction, not the publicity.

items.explanation: Industrial cities did cluster workers near factories around a downtown of offices and banks, with saloons in working-class wards — but by 1890 steam, not water, powered most industry.
options: A. Workers lived near factories close to downtown
B. Factories were sited near water for power
C. Downtowns held offices, banks, and insurers
D. Saloons dotted working-class neighborhoods
items.stem: All of the following describe the late-nineteenth-century industrial city EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: True of the era: industrial workers really did live near factories close to downtown, since they walked to work. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Correct — this is the exception. By 1890 steam engines, not waterpower, drove most industry, so factories no longer had to sit beside rivers for power. Water-powered mill towns belonged to an earlier industrial era.
option_explanations.C: True of the era: downtowns really did hold offices, banks, and insurers while workers lived in wards around them. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.D: True of the era: saloons really did dot working-class neighborhoods, serving as social centers for immigrant workers. This is not the exception.

items.explanation: Real wages rose faster than living costs for many workers — the truest measure of improvement, since new consumer goods meant little to those who couldn't afford them.
options: A. Comparing wage gains against rising living costs
B. Cataloging the new foods available in stores
C. Counting new amusement parks and theaters
D. Comparing immigrant wages with wages back home
items.stem: The best evidence that working-class living standards improved in this era comes from

option_explanations.A: Correct. Comparing wage gains against rising living costs — real wages — is the truest measure of whether workers could actually buy more. Rising money wages mean little if prices rose faster.
option_explanations.B: New foods in stores show that new goods existed, not that workers could afford them. Availability is not the same as a rising standard of living for working people.
option_explanations.C: Amusement parks and theaters show new leisure existed, but not who could afford it. Counting entertainment venues cannot tell you whether a worker's real income rose.
option_explanations.D: Comparing immigrant wages with wages back home tells you why immigrants came — wages were higher than in the old country — but not whether American workers' living standards improved over time. It answers a migration question, not a living-standards question.

items.explanation: Tarbell builds her case on the money: dividends 'averaging about forty-five million dollars a year, or nearly fifty per cent. on its capitalisation,' a sum 'capitalised at five per cent.' yielding $900,000,000, with 'ninety per cent.' flowing to the Standard Oil 'family.' The indictment is arithmetic -- concentration of wealth -- not interviews, price statistics, or anecdotes.
options: A. Interviews with John D. Rockefeller himself
B. Financial data on dividends, profits, and capitalization
C. Government statistics on consumer oil prices
D. Personal anecdotes about oil workers
items.stem: In the passage, Tarbell's argument against Standard Oil rests primarily on
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"The profits of the present Standard Oil Company are enormous. For five years the dividends have been averaging about forty-five million dollars a year... a sum which, if distributed among the thousands of stockholders, would make every one of them rich — and yet the company was built up by methods which have made it the most hated corporation in the country."
—Ida Tarbell, on Standard Oil, 1904 (abridged and paraphrased)

option_explanations.A: Tarbell never interviewed Rockefeller for the piece — the passage builds its case from the company's money, not from conversations with its founder.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The passage's argument is built on financial data: dividends 'averaging about forty-five million dollars a year,' nearly fifty percent on capitalization, ninety percent flowing to the Standard Oil 'family.' The indictment is arithmetic — concentration of wealth — not interviews, price statistics, or anecdotes.
option_explanations.C: The passage never cites government statistics on consumer oil prices. Tarbell's charge is about how much wealth concentrated in a few hands, not about what consumers paid.
option_explanations.D: The passage contains no personal anecdotes about oil workers. Tarbell builds the case from dividends, profits, and capitalization figures — financial evidence, not stories.

items.explanation: Tarbell's point is concentration: 'probably ninety per cent.' of the immense revenue 'goes to the few men who make up the Standard Oil family,' and 'it must every year be invested' -- wealth piling up in fewer and fewer hands, year after year. She says nothing of falling consumer prices, thriving competitors, or withheld dividends.
options: A. A handful of men controlled enormous revenues that had to be reinvested yearly
B. Oil prices fell steadily to benefit consumers
C. Independent competitors thrived alongside the trust
D. The company paid no dividends to its owners
items.stem: According to the passage, Standard Oil's dominance meant that
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"The profits of the present Standard Oil Company are enormous. For five years the dividends have been averaging about forty-five million dollars a year... a sum which, if distributed among the thousands of stockholders, would make every one of them rich — and yet the company was built up by methods which have made it the most hated corporation in the country."
—Ida Tarbell, on Standard Oil, 1904 (abridged and paraphrased)

option_explanations.A: Correct. Tarbell's point is concentration: 'probably ninety per cent.' of the immense revenue goes to the few men who make up the Standard Oil 'family,' and the money 'must every year be invested' — wealth piling up in fewer and fewer hands, year after year.
option_explanations.B: The passage says nothing about oil prices falling for consumers. Tarbell's subject is the concentration of revenue and control, not consumer prices.
option_explanations.C: The opposite of the passage's picture. Standard Oil's dominance crushed independent competitors — Tarbell describes concentration in a few hands, not thriving rivals alongside the trust.
option_explanations.D: The passage says the opposite: Standard Oil paid enormous dividends — about $45 million a year for five years. The charge is about who got those dividends (a few men), not that none were paid.

items.explanation: Tarbell's History ran in McClure's (1902-1904) and became ammunition for the Progressive assault on the trusts. In 1911 the Supreme Court, applying the Sherman Antitrust Act, dissolved Standard Oil into 34 separate companies -- the direct legislative and judicial answer to the concentration she documented.
options: A. The repeal of all federal business regulation
B. Rockefeller's election to the presidency
C. Progressive Era antitrust action culminating in the 1911 breakup of Standard Oil
D. The nationalization of the American oil industry
items.stem: The concentration of power Tarbell describes helped produce which of the following?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"The profits of the present Standard Oil Company are enormous. For five years the dividends have been averaging about forty-five million dollars a year... a sum which, if distributed among the thousands of stockholders, would make every one of them rich — and yet the company was built up by methods which have made it the most hated corporation in the country."
—Ida Tarbell, on Standard Oil, 1904 (abridged and paraphrased)

option_explanations.A: The opposite of what happened. Tarbell's expose fueled demands for more federal business regulation, not less — her work helped bring on the Progressive Era's antitrust and regulatory push.
option_explanations.B: Rockefeller never ran for president. The political result of Tarbell's work was not his election but the legal attack on his company.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Tarbell's History of the Standard Oil Company (1902–1904) became ammunition for the Progressive assault on the trusts; in 1911 the Supreme Court, applying the Sherman Antitrust Act, dissolved Standard Oil into 34 separate companies.
option_explanations.D: The American oil industry was never nationalized. The government's answer was breaking Standard Oil up through antitrust law, not taking it over.
